definitions.text: The reproduction that does not involve the fusion of gametes is called asexual reproduction.
The reproduction that involves the fusion of male and female gametes is called sexual reproduction.
Binary fission means division in to two.
During budding, a part of the parent organism grows out from its body. This part is called a bud.
Spores are thick-walled asexual reproductive cells.
It is a methods of asexual reproduction in plants. In this method, new plant is produced from the vegetative part (root, stem or leaf) of the parent plant.
Natural vegetative propagation is a process where plants reproduce on their own, using structures like stems, roots, or leaves.
Artificial vegetative propagation means the processes in which humans use the vegetative parts of plants for their reproduction by methods like cuttings, grafting, or layering.
It is a horizontal stem that grows above the ground. A stolon has nodes where new leaves and roots grow.
It is fleshy stem that grows underground. It has “eyes” which are actually its buds.
It is a horizontal stem that grows below the ground. It has nodes where new leaves and roots grow.
It is a very short stem that grows underground. It has bud and fleshy leaves.
It resembles the bulb but does not have fleshy leaves. Almost all of a corm consists of stem, with a few brown non-functional leaves on the outside.
Suckers are new shoots that emerge from the base of the parent plant or from its underground roots. These shoots grow into new plants while still attached to the parent.
Such a piece of stem or root that are cut from a plant and used to grow new plant is called cutting.
Grafting is the joining of two or more plant parts of the same type to form a single plant.
The sporophyte generation produces spores which grow and make the new gametophyte generation.
The gametophyte generation produces gametes which unite and make the new sporophyte generation.
This phenomenon is called alternation of generations.
The receptacle is the swollen tip of a flower stalk where all the floral parts (are attached. It serves as the base that supports the flower's structure.
It is the outermost whorl. It is made of green leaf-like sepals. Sepals protect the inner parts of a developing flower before it opens.
It is the second whorl and made of petals. Most flowers have coloured petals.
It is the third whorl and is made of male reproductive structures called stamens. Each stamen consists of an anther and a filament.
It is the innermost whorl made of the female reproductive structures called carpels. A carpel consists of three parts.
It is called pollination i.e. the transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma.
The transfer of pollens from the anther to the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant is called self-pollination.
The transfer of pollens from the anther of one plant to the stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species. is called cross-pollination.
This process of the fusion of two sperms (one with the egg and the other with the fusion nucleus) is called double fertilization.
This process is known as parthenocarpy.
The resulting structure, which contains seven cells (one egg cell, one fusion nucleus, and five non-functional cells), is the female gametophyte or embryo sac.
The resulting two-celled structure is a pollen grain, which is the male gametophyte.

formulas.formula: Sporophyte (2n) → meiosis → spores (1n) → gametophyte (1n) → gametes (1n) → fertilization → zygote (2n) → sporophyte (2n)
formulas.use: Use to show alternation of generations; n means a chromosome-set count, so it is dimensionless and has no SI unit.
Use for fusion of haploid nuclei to form a diploid nucleus, such as the egg and sperm forming a zygote; n is a dimensionless chromosome-set count.
Use for the second sperm fusing with the fusion nucleus to form the triploid endosperm nucleus; n is a dimensionless chromosome-set count.

fullMarks: For binary fission, write the stages in order: bacterial DNA replicates, daughter DNA molecules move to opposite sides, the membrane pinches in, a new cell wall forms in the middle, and two identical daughter bacteria result.
For vegetative structures, identify whether each is above or below ground, describe the relevant buds or nodes, and add an example plant where asked.
For artificial propagation, define cutting and grafting separately, explain how each is done, and include examples such as roses or grapevines for cuttings and fruit trees for grafting.
For flower questions, list all four whorls in order from outermost to innermost, then give each whorl’s components; label anther, filament, stigma, style, ovary, petal and sepal clearly on a diagram.

For embryo-sac development, show the number and ploidy of the starting cell and products: one diploid megaspore mother cell, four haploid megaspores, one surviving megaspore, then eight haploid nuclei; finish with the egg, fusion nucleus and five non-functional cells.

For the flowering-plant life cycle, connect the stages with arrows and include meiosis, mitosis, pollination, fertilization, seed formation and the next sporophyte; keep 1n, 2n and 3n labels accurate.

When explaining double fertilization, state what each sperm fuses with and what each product becomes: egg forms the zygote and then embryo; fusion nucleus forms the endosperm nucleus and then endosperm.
End each explanation by directly answering the question, and use the book’s terms such as microspore, megaspore, gametophyte, sporophyte and embryo sac accurately.
mistakes: Mixing up a stolon and a rhizome. Fix: a stolon is a horizontal stem above ground; a rhizome is a horizontal stem below ground.
Writing that potato is a root tuber. Fix: the chapter describes a tuber as a fleshy underground stem, and potato eyes are buds.
Saying bulbs and corms both have fleshy leaves. Fix: a bulb has fleshy leaves; a corm does not.
Confusing cutting with grafting. Fix: a cutting is a piece of stem or root used to grow a plant; grafting joins plant parts to form one plant.
Calling the pollen grain the female gametophyte or the embryo sac the male gametophyte. Fix: pollen grain is male; embryo sac is female.
Giving the wrong products of double fertilization. Fix: one sperm fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote; the other fuses with the fusion nucleus to form a triploid nucleus.
Leaving out the ploidy or the number of embryo-sac products. Fix: include four haploid megaspores, one surviving megaspore, eight haploid nuclei, and the final seven-cell structure.

shortTheory.question: Write a short note on budding in yeast.
shortTheory.answer: This method is very common in yeast (a unicellular fungus). During budding, a part of the parent organism grows out from its body. This part is called a bud. When the bud has grown big, it may separate from parent body or may remain attached.

shortTheory.question: Write a short note on spore formation in fungi.
shortTheory.answer: Spores are thick-walled asexual reproductive cells. Most fungi (e.g. Rhizopus: bread mold) produce spores in special sac-like structures called sporangia (Singular: sporangium). When spores are mature, the sporangium bursts and spores are released. Spores can tolerate unfavourable conditions due to their thick walls. When favourable conditions are available, the spores germinate to produce new fungus.

shortTheory.question: Describe how vegetative propagation occurs through runners.
shortTheory.answer: Stolon (runner): It is a horizontal stem that grows above the ground. A stolon has nodes where new leaves and roots grow. The leaves grow upwards and roots grow down. In this way, a new plant is formed at the node. Strawberry reproduces by using its stolon.

shortTheory.question: State how potatoes reproduce through tubers.
shortTheory.answer: Tuber: It is fleshy stem that grows underground. It has “eyes” which are actually its buds. Eyes can grow into new plants. Potatoes reproduce by tubers.

shortTheory.question: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of vegetative propagation.
shortTheory.answer: Vegetative propagation allows to produce many new plants in a short time. The new plants are exactly like the parent plant, so they all have the same good characteristics. This means useful qualities, like good fruit or strong growth, are passed on to the next generation. Plants produced through vegetative propagation do not have genetic differences. In other words, all the offspring are identical. Due to it, they are equally sensitive to environmental changes and prone to the same diseases or pests.

shortTheory.question: Name the four whorls present in a flower and tell the components of each whorl.
shortTheory.answer: Calyx: It is the outermost whorl. It is made of green leaf-like sepals. Corolla: It is the second whorl and made of petals. Androecium: It is the third whorl and is made of male reproductive structures called stamens. Each stamen consists of an anther and a filament. Gynoecium: It is the innermost whorl made of the female reproductive structures called carpels. A carpel consists of three parts: ovary, style and stigma.

shortTheory.question: Briefly describe the formation of egg cell and polar nuclei within the embryo sac.
shortTheory.answer: The ovule acts as megasporangium. It contains a diploid megaspore mother cell which undergoes meiosis and produces four haploid megaspores. Only one megaspore remains alive. Inside megaspore, eight haploid nuclei are formed by mitosis. Two nuclei migrate to the center and fuse to form a fusion nucleus. One nucleus out of the remaining six forms the female gamete i.e., egg cell.

shortTheory.question: Differentiate between asexual and sexual reproduction.
shortTheory.answer: The reproduction that does not involve the fusion of gametes is called asexual reproduction. The offspring produced by asexual reproduction are genetically identical to the parents. On the other hand, the reproduction that involves the fusion of male and female gametes is called sexual reproduction. In sexual reproduction, the offspring have variations among themselves and with the parents.
